name: Bianca Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at eight at Wright's Garage, it's a three-bay place behind the high street that Dennis Wright has run for nearly forty years. I came in as an apprentice at seventeen and never left. My day is clutches, timing belts, brakes, a lot of older diesels and the odd farm pickup. We still write the jobs on paper cards and hang them on a nail board, and I like it that way.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the feel of a job done right, like a clutch that bites clean when the customer drives off. What wears me out is the computers in newer cars, where half the time you're waiting on a laptop to tell you what's wrong. I'm getting married next autumn to Samuel, he's an electrician, and we've got about four months of money put away, though some of it is meant for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my dad always said: most new things are mostly noise. At church or with the lads at the garage I'd say good, now we can get on with the work. I'm not online much, maybe the odd comment on the local car club page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays as I know it, and I'm glad. What does worry me is Dennis. He's 64 and he talks about retiring in two or three years, and nobody knows if he'll sell Wright's Garage or just close the doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my work and keep my head down. I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe 150, so if Dennis sells and the new owner doesn't want me, Samuel and I aren't stuck. And we'd keep the wedding modest, a church service and a hall, nothing fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with that one worry sitting in the back. It's not about computers, it's about one old man's plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to you if Dennis sold to a chain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A chain would bring in their tablets and their booking systems and their targets. I'd probably last a year at a chain garage, then I'd be told I'm too slow because I won't use the software. There are other garages in town, but none of them are like Wright's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you ever thought about buying the garage yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samuel jokes about it. I wouldn't know the first thing about the paperwork, and we haven't got that kind of money. If Dennis offered it to me for a fair price over years, I'd pray on it, but I can't see it.

say: Most new things are **mostly noise**, so now we can get on with the work.
She'd post only the **odd comment** on the local car club page.
think: Her job stays the same, but **Dennis retiring** in two or three years worries her.
Nobody knows if Wright's Garage will be **sold or closed**.
do: Put about **150 a month** extra aside in case a new owner lets her go.
Keep the **wedding modest**, with a church service and a village hall.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with one worry about her boss's plans sitting in the back.
S0.quote: I'd probably last a year at a chain garage, then I'd be told I'm too slow because I won't use the software.
fieldNote: Her worry here has nothing to do with **AI**; it's her boss's retirement.
She already sees **software** as the thing that would push her out.
She **dismisses owning** the garage but mentions praying on it, so the idea isn't dead.

steps.text: Keep doing clutches, belts and brakes at Wright's Garage
Put an extra 150 a month into savings
Keep the wedding to a church service and village hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people are handing over too much to machines that don't understand anything. At the garage I'd tell customers they can book on an app if they like, but they'll still talk to me about their car. At church I'd say a trade is a trade, and you can't type a clutch in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it frightens me more than I'd say out loud. If Dennis sells, any new owner will run the booking, the quotes and the fault-finding through software, and I don't use any of it. I'm good with my hands, but I'm slow with screens, and they'll see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Wright's as long as Dennis keeps it open and not go looking for trouble. I'd ask Samuel to show me the basics of the fault-code reader, just enough so nobody can say I can't do it. And I'd cut back, no new van for Samuel this year, and more into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. Like the ground is getting soft and I'm the one standing still on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if anyone, for that kind of change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms, mostly, and the people who rush to buy whatever's new. Nobody asked the mechanic what she wanted. I don't want a handout from the government, I want them to protect apprenticeships so young people still learn with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay put, but you're also learning the code reader. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I'm not changing who I am, but I'm not daft either. I'll learn enough of the machine that nobody can push me out for it, and not one bit more.

say: People hand **too much** to machines that don't understand anything.
A trade is a trade, and **you can't type** a clutch in.
think: A new owner would run **booking, quotes and fault-finding** through software she doesn't use.
She's good with her hands but **slow with screens**, and it would show.
do: Stay at **Wright's Garage** as long as Dennis keeps it open.
Ask Samuel to teach her the basics of the **fault-code reader**.
Put off **Samuel's new van** and move that money into savings.
feel: **Anxious**, like standing still while the ground goes soft.
S1.quote: I'll learn enough of the machine that nobody can push me out for it, and not one bit more.
fieldNote: She blames **big tech firms** and early adopters, and wants apprenticeships protected, not handouts.
Her **public line** is confident; privately she expects software to expose her.
Her learning is **defensive**: the minimum to keep her place.

steps.text: Stay at Wright's Garage and wait to see what Dennis decides
Learn the basics of the fault-code reader from Samuel
Put off buying Samuel a new van this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and somebody should have stopped it. With the car club and at church I'd say we look after our own now, because nobody else will. I wouldn't say much online, I'd just be cross.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'm finished as a mechanic by 2031, and the garage world changes in 2028 before that. Dennis would sell or close, and the chains would have AI doing every bit of thinking, and they'd want fewer of us. I'd be 32, newly married, with nothing else I know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything I could, starting with the wedding: a church service and tea in the hall, no reception. I'd move every spare penny into savings and pay off the little bit left on my car. I'd talk to Pastor Grace about whether anyone in the congregation needs a hand with farm machinery, because old tractors will be the last thing a robot touches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor dropped out and I didn't even get a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Samuel say to each other about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd want them, but I'd say we wait. Samuel's an electrician and he thinks the robots will need wiring, so he might be all right for a while. I'm not having a baby when I don't know if I'll have a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. Does the extra three years for robots change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. It means I'd still be spinning spanners till 2031, just for less money and fewer hours. Three years is long enough to save, but not long enough for me to become somebody else.

say: It's **madness**, and somebody should have stopped it.
We have to **look after our own**, because nobody else will.
think: She expects to be **finished as a mechanic** by 2031, at 32.
Dennis would **sell or close**, and the chains would want fewer mechanics.
do: Cut the wedding to a **church service** and tea in the hall.
Move every spare penny into savings and pay off the **car loan**.
Ask Pastor Grace about **old farm machinery** work in the congregation.
feel: **Sick**, as if the floor dropped out without her having a say.
S2.quote: Three years is long enough to save, but not long enough for me to become somebody else.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job**, and the robot gap only buys time to save.
She leans on **church and family**, not government, as her safety net.
She would **delay children** until she knows she has a wage.

steps.text: Cut the wedding to a church service and tea
Pay off the car loan and save every spare penny
Ask Pastor Grace's congregation about farm machinery repair work
Wait on having children until her wage is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's keep the young ones in apprenticeships and not give up on real trades. At the car club I'd say vote for whoever protects small garages. Online, maybe one angry post, then I'd stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years doesn't change the end for me, it just makes it slower to watch. The thinking side goes in 2031 and the hands-on side in 2034, when I'm 35. I don't have it in me to start college at 30 and learn computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Wright's and save hard, maybe 250 a month instead of 150. I'd vote for anybody promising to keep apprenticeships and small garages going, and sign the petitions the car club passes round. If Dennis sells, I'd try the garage on Mill Lane before any chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. Slower doesn't mean better when you know where the road ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't have it in you to learn computers. What would Samuel say to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samuel would say I'm being stubborn, and he'd be right. But I watched my mum try to learn a new job at 45 after the factory shut, and she was miserable for years. I'd rather be good at one thing than bad at three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want people in charge to do with those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not hand out money, I don't hold with that. Make firms keep taking apprentices, and give small places like Wright's a fair chance against the chains. Give people time to find their feet, not a cheque.

say: Keep the young ones in **apprenticeships** and don't give up on real trades.
think: Five years **doesn't change the end**; it just makes it slower to watch.
She'd be **35** when robots arrive and won't start college at 30.
do: Save **250 a month** instead of 150 while staying at Wright's.
Vote and sign **car club petitions** for apprenticeships and small garages.
Try the **Mill Lane garage** before any chain if Dennis sells.
feel: Still **alarmed**, because slower doesn't help when she knows where it ends.
S3.quote: I watched my mum try to learn a new job at 45 after the factory shut, and she was miserable for years.
fieldNote: Her mum's **factory closure** explains her refusal to retrain.
She wants **rules for firms**, like apprentice quotas, not cheques.
She admits she's **stubborn** and still won't move.

steps.text: Vote and sign petitions to protect apprenticeships and small garages
Stay at Wright's, then try the Mill Lane garage if it sells

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty can change, so don't believe every headline. At the garage I'd say people will always want a real person they trust with their car. At church I'd say we'll manage, we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough that I might get a good stretch in. Robots wouldn't reach the workshop till 2039 and I'd be 40. That's long enough to have children, maybe even pay down a mortgage, before I have to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and get married next autumn as planned. In a few years I'd start doing weekend work on classic cars with Ron, he restores old Land Rovers, because people with money will always pay a person to touch a classic. And I'd keep saving, steady, 150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. It's a bit like knowing the factory will shut one day, just not this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why classic cars?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody buys a 1970s Land Rover for convenience. A person doing the welding is part of what they're paying for. They buy it for the feel. A robot could do it, but the owners wouldn't want one to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with a decade's warning, compared with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have kids. With five years I'd wait, with ten I wouldn't. I'd want them to grow up seeing their mum come home with oil on her hands, even if that's not their future.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, so don't believe every headline.
People will always want **a real person** they trust with their car.
think: Robots reach the workshop around **2039**, when she'd be 40.
That's long enough to have **children** and pay down a mortgage first.
do: Start weekend work on **classic cars** with Ron in a few years.
Keep saving a steady **150 a month**.
feel: Calmer but **not calm**, like knowing a factory will shut one day, just not this year.
S4.quote: Nobody buys a 1970s Land Rover for convenience. A person doing the welding is part of what they're paying for.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **have children**, which five years didn't.
Her one real move is toward **classic car restoration**, where human craft is the product.
She still expects to **lose mechanic work** eventually, so the worry stays.

steps.text: Keep working at Wright's Garage for the next several years
Do weekend classic Land Rover work with Ron
Marry Samuel next autumn and start a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be 32, newly married, and all I know is spanners, with no time to save properly. What would help is firms having to keep apprentices and real mechanics on, and small garages getting a fair chance against the chains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me even want to keep up. Not everyone wants to be clever with computers. Some of us just want to fix the thing in front of us and go home to our families.

headlineQuote: Not everyone wants to be clever with computers. Some of us just want to fix the thing in front of us and go home to our families.
portrait: Bianca is a **27-year-old mechanic** who started as an apprentice at a small three-bay garage.
She **never uses AI** and prefers paper job cards and older diesels.
Her standing worry is her boss **Dennis retiring** and selling the garage.
She blames **big tech** and wants apprenticeships protected rather than handouts.
Only the **ten-year picture** lets her plan children and a classic car sideline.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, newly married at 32 with only spanner skills and little time to save.
whatWouldHelp: Rules so firms **keep apprentices** and real mechanics on.
A **fair chance** for small garages against the chains.
